chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a person in Ihram who caught an ostrich or a wild donkey. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him is a Bant camel.' I said, 'If he cannot afford a Bant camel?' He said: 'So let him feed sixty poor people.' I said, 'If he cannot afford to give charity?' He said: 'So let him fast eighteen days, and the charity is one Mudd for each poor person.'

He (the narrator) said, 'And I asked him about a person in Ihram who caught a cow. He said: 'Upon him is a cow.' I said, 'If he cannot afford a cow?' He said: 'So let him feed thirty poor people.' I said, 'If he cannot afford to give charity?' He said: 'So let him fast nine days.'

I said, 'If he catches a gazelle?' He said: 'Upon him is a sheep.' I said, 'If he cannot afford it?' He said: 'So the feeding of ten poor people. If he cannot afford what he should give in charity, then upon him is the fasting of three days.'

key_terms.بَدَنَةٌ: A young female camel, one year old
key_terms.مُحْرِمٌ: A person in the state of Ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)
key_terms.مُدٌّ: A traditional unit of volume for dry food, approximately 750 grams

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for hunting while in Ihram according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the specific expiations (kaffarah) for hunting wild game while in Ihram, establishing a graded scale of compensation based on the animal's size and the individual's financial capacity. It highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of substituting animal sacrifice with feeding the poor (sixty muds for an ostrich) and fasting, reflecting the practical adaptability of divine law. The narration underscores the importance of proportional justice in ritual penalties, linking physical sacrifice to spiritual purification through fasting.
